item.title: When Do You Need a Christian Therapist?
item.description:
With recent events, more people are turning back to their Christian faith or discovering Jesus for the first time. Christian counseling is about helping people find ways to improve their mental health through a biblical perspective. Jesus broke His people free from the yokes and burdens of this life to live for Him, so we know we can break unhealthy and generational cycles through Him. A Christian therapist can get you on the right path toward healing.

Why People Choose a Christian Therapist

People inherently know there is more to life, even if they are unsure what it can be. We were made to worship something or someone. God created this innate desire to draw us closer to Him. Often, we get off track by the world and need help resetting our priorities. Yet, it is God who can heal us of every temptation and sin. We can lean on Him when we feel anxious, depressed, or out of control.

Topics Covered in Christian Therapy

Christian counseling covers a wide range of topics from family issues to severe mental health disorders. A Christian therapist specializes in specific areas and can bring their expertise to the session, combining evidence-based methods with faith-based principles. This combination helps people overcome problems while growing emotionally, mentally, and spiritually.

The following are several topics covered through Christian counseling.

Trauma

Trauma can occur after a sudden event or through long-term exposure. For example, a person may suffer the effects of trauma after a natural disaster or house fire. They can experience trauma after witnessing a crime or caring for a terminal loved one. The body’s response to trauma is to activate the fight-or-flight response, which can lead to anxiety disorders and depression.

Abandonment and Neglect

Abandonment and neglect during childhood can often lead to adult problems with self-esteem, confidence, and relationships. Children may withdraw or lash out as they try to find their place in this world and feel loved. This can lead to behavioral problems and depression.

Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD)

Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD with or without hyperactivity) can interfere with school, work, and relationships. Adults learn to cover up the symptoms of ADHD, but can still feel out of control and forgetful. Children with ADHD may feel misunderstood.

Anger Issues

Anger management is offered through a Christian therapist. Anger issues can stem from childhood, hormonal changes, or mental health disorders. Learning how to calm oneself and resolve conflict peacefully is a lifelong skill one can learn.

Anxiety

Anxious thoughts and worries can develop into anxiety disorders and Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder (OCD). The Bible tells us hundreds of times not to fear, and Jesus told us not to worry about tomorrow, yet our minds require constant renewing because we give in so easily to anxiety. Chemical imbalances in the brain can also contribute to high anxiety.

Depression

Depression can be dangerous if left untreated. Most people feel blue at least sometimes during their lifetime. However, depression can feel permanent and last for several weeks or months. It can lead to intrusive thoughts, self-harm, or suicide. Depression is often seen in teens and adults, although some children who have suffered trauma or abuse may develop depression.

Eating Disorders

Anorexia nervosa, bulimia, and binge eating are eating disorders that, if left untreated, can be fatal. In the case of anorexia, the body starves as nutrients are withheld. Eventually, this leads to organ failure. Bulimia, bingeing and purging food, can lead to physical conditions that endanger life. Binge eating can lead to problems, such as high blood pressure, high cholesterol, heart attack, stroke, Type 2 diabetes, obesity, and a loss of self-worth.

Autism Spectrum Disorder

The autism spectrum is wide, and not everyone develops the same signs. Christian counseling can help children and adults move forward and not allow autism to be a barrier. People with autism can learn how to communicate, navigate social cues, and regulate emotions through therapy.

Bipolar Disorder

Bipolar disorder consists of manic episodes (highs) and depressive episodes (lows). This cycle can last weeks or months. In some cases, people with bipolar disorder may cycle quickly between manic and depressive states, which can confuse others at home, work, and in relationships.

Substance Abuse

Alcohol and drugs, including prescription drugs, can lead to addiction if abused. Substance abuse becomes a problem when you use it as a coping mechanism. These substances can lead to mental and physical issues, deteriorate relationships, and endanger your job.

Physical and Sexual Abuse

No one should ever experience physical, verbal, or sexual abuse. Yet, we live in a fallen world, and far too many people have suffered at the hands of others. Christian counseling is customized to your needs. Your Christian therapist will work with you to remove the power left behind by memories and words and replace them with the power of Jesus. You will learn strategies to overcome your past and move away from current toxic relationships.

Marriage or Relationship Problems

Every relationship or marriage has its issues. Learning to walk through them together can be hard. Christian counseling addresses premarital, relationship, and marriage problems. Areas that Christian therapists often work with clients on include premarital expectations, boundaries for in-laws, infidelity and affairs, financial strain, parenting disagreements, addiction, and grief.

Grief and Loss

Grief and loss can weigh one down. The grieving process is not linear. It consists of denial and shock, anger, bargaining, depression, and acceptance. However, most people cycle through these stages several times, often staying in one stage longer than the others. When grief or loss interferes with your daily responsibilities and mental health over time, you may need a Christian therapist to help you cope and heal.

Family Issues

Family issues can vary from moving to a new city and schools to problems between parents or parents and children. Blended families may need family counseling to address the issues that can arise when two households become one. Family counseling is also helpful when one member of the family is struggling with a mental disorder, as the others learn how to support and encourage them.

Men’s and Women’s Issues

Counseling covers the areas that cause you the most concern, even the ones you might deem embarrassing. Christian counselors work with professionalism and want to help you overcome these issues. Counselors may work with men having erectile problems that interfere with their marriage, men and women struggling with the temptation of an emotional affair, or a woman admitting that she feels a distance from her children. Counseling is a safe space for these hard conversations.

Teen Problems

Teens have their own issues that impact their lives and families. Teen pregnancy, bullying, peer pressure, premarital sex, not feeling accepted, drug abuse, online predators, and targeted internet attacks can rob a child of their self-esteem and leave them confused. They can feel as if the weight of the world is on their shoulders. Teens who have experienced trauma or abuse may develop anxiety and depression. Teens are also at a higher risk of self-harm and suicide.

Spiritual Growth

Spiritual growth provides you with a foundation in the Word, knowledge about God, and a personal relationship with Jesus. It equips you to share the gospel with a hurt and fallen world. Spiritual growth helps you to rely on and trust that God has a bigger plan for your greater good. A Christian therapist will help you align your life to Scripture and follow Jesus, seeking God before making big decisions and turning your worries and hurts over to Him.

Finding a Christian Therapist in Your Area

If you are looking for a Christian therapist in your area, contact our team today. A representative will connect you with a Christian therapist. We offer virtual sessions to clients who may find it more relaxing to confide in the comfort of their own home. We also hold in-person and group counseling sessions. Call us today to learn more about how a Christian therapist and counseling can help you.

item.title: When Borderline Traits Go Unnoticed: The Hidden Patterns That Shape Daily Life
item.description:
We often think of mental health challenges as being a clear diagnosis with obvious symptoms. However, there are times when the signs are subtle. Borderline traits are one of those challenges that can exist beneath the surface, shaping relationships, emotions, and decision-making without ever being recognized for what they are.

Borderline traits are often dismissed as personality, quirks, or emotional sensitivity. The person experiencing them may feel like something is off, but they don’t know how to name it. These traits don’t always meet the threshold for a formal diagnosis, so they remain in the background, affecting daily life in ways that feel confusing and isolating.

Understanding these hidden patterns begins with asking what lies beneath them that feels familiar and frustrating. It’s a journey of curiosity and not judgment. In faith, you can come to God and ask for help:

Search me, O God, and know my heart! Try me and know my thoughts! – Psalm 139:23, ESV

Borderline Traits and Emotional Intensity

The most common appearance of borderline traits is in the intensity of emotional responses. A minor disagreement can feel like a complete rupture, and a moment of perceived rejection can trigger overwhelming shame or anger. These involuntary reactions arise with a force that feels beyond control.

After experiencing these reactions, individuals often wonder why they responded so strongly. Friends and family often describe them as overly sensitive or dramatic, unaware that what they are witnessing is a nervous system that processes emotions at a heightened level.

The intensity goes beyond negative feelings. Joy can feel explosive, and excitement can quickly turn into anxiety. It is as if the individual experiences emotions without a dimmer switch, and everything is at full volume. The result is exhaustion for the person experiencing it and for those around them. This constant navigation of highs and lows becomes a way of life that feels normal even when it’s depleting.

Christian counselors recognize emotional intensity as a sign that the nervous system, from early on, learned to stay vigilant. The individual learns to read every signal as potentially dangerous. Healing from borderline traits and the intensity of emotions involves learning to regulate what feels uncontrollable and find safety in the presence of God and people you trust. God is faithful to help you in this place:

He heals the brokenhearted and binds up their wounds. – Psalm 147:3, ESV

Borderline Traits and the Fear of Abandonment in Relationships

Persistent fear that people will leave is one of the most painful aspects of undetected borderline traits. This is a deep dread that influences decisions, communications, and attachment. It is common for these individuals to repeatedly test relationships by pushing people away to see if they’ll come back.

Another response is to cling to people, fearing that any space will result in a permanent loss. Each response stems from the same core belief that they are fundamentally unworthy of staying.

It’s not a fear that is always present and clear. It could look like jealousy, control, or a constant need for reassurance. It may show up as an inability to be alone or, conversely, as a pattern of ending relationships before the other person has had a chance to leave first. It is a desperate attempt to avoid the pain of abandonment, even when the avoidance creates the very distance that they have feared.

Recognizing the fear is the first step toward addressing it. The process requires the individual to acknowledge how past experiences of loss or inconsistency have created a template for how their relationships feel. They have to learn to build new experiences that challenge the assumption that everyone will eventually leave.

The Unstable Sense of Self that Shifts with Circumstances

Those who struggle with undetected borderline traits often feel as if they do not know who they are. They also feel their sense of identity shift depending on who they are with, what role they play, or what feedback they receive. This is not an intentional deception. It is a genuine question about their own values, preferences, and personality.

Some individuals may adopt their romantic partner’s interests, only to change their minds when the relationship ends. These individuals often change career plans frequently in search of the right thing, but never quite find it.

The result of this unstable sense of self is a chronic feeling of emptiness. It is a sense of a core lacking that other people seem to have. This makes decision-making difficult because they lack an internal compass to provide guidance. These individuals often look to others for validation and try to piece together their identity from external feedback rather than from internal knowing.

Christian counselors help these individuals explore their identity in Christ. Together, they can lay a foundation that does not shift with circumstances and creates a stable reference point when everything else feels uncertain. This process involves separating what has been absorbed by the experiences from what is genuinely true for them.

The Impulsive Behaviors that Offer Temporary Relief

Impulsive behaviors offer a moment of relief when emotions feel unbearable, and the sense of self feels shaky. These behaviors may include spending money recklessly, engaging in risky sexual behavior, substance abuse, binge eating, or self-harm to name a few.

The function of the behavior is to provide a temporary escape from their experience of emotional pain or emptiness. It may feel that the behaviors are the only option at the time. Afterward, there is often shame and regret, which fuels more emotional pain and possibly more impulsive behavior.

These patterns are hard to address because they work temporarily. They become automatic responses to distress, which do provide relief but also reinforce impulsive behavior. The individuals who struggle with borderline traits may not even recognize the patterns of these behaviors until they are brought to their attention, or the consequences can no longer be ignored.

Breaking free from these impulsive patterns requires that an individual develop healthier ways to manage distress. This includes learning to tolerate uncomfortable emotions instead of immediately seeking escape. It is slow work that requires patience and support. It is encouraging to remember Scripture in this case:

No temptation has overtaken you that is not common to man. God is faithful, and he will not let you be tempted beyond your ability, but with the temptation he will also provide the way of escape, that you may be able to endure it. – 1 Corinthians 10:13, ESV

Finding Clarity and Hope

Understanding and recognizing undetected borderline traits does not involve assigning a label. The goal is to find clarity for patterns that have felt confusing when someone cannot name what they have been experiencing. This will open the door to getting help and reduce the blame they place upon themselves for being too much or not enough. It gives them a pathway to address the underlying patterns with compassion and effective strategies.

This process involves therapy approaches such as dialectical behavior therapy to target emotional regulation, distress tolerance, and interpersonal effectiveness. Building a support system that can hold steady when emotions feel chaotic is another part of the process to address these traits. Deepening a relationship with God, who offers unconditional love, creates a foundation that does not shift with behavior or performance.

For I am sure that neither death nor life, nor angels nor rulers, nor things present nor things to come, nor powers, nor height nor depth, nor anything else in all creation, will be able to separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord. – Romans 8:38-39, ESV

Taking the Next Step

Recognizing that you struggle with borderline trait patterns is a start toward better mental health. Reaching out for professional help is a crucial step, and it is not a weakness or failure. It’s important to find support that will encourage your journey toward healing through a faith-based process. Christian counselors are equipped to help you understand and identify borderline trait patterns and behavior.

Contact our reception team to learn more about your options and get started working with someone who can help you navigate emotional regulation and relationship patterns.

item.title: Emotional Burnout and the Hidden Guilt of Rest
item.description:
Not every kind of depletion announces itself right away; some just quietly settle in and stay. It builds up slowly in the early mornings and late nights. Lingering in the days that you pushed through, even though your body was screaming for rest.

When you decide to listen to your body, you find that instead of relief, you are faced with feelings of guilt, as if you are falling behind on something. It’s as if you have to earn rest before you are allowed to experience it. This is emotional burnout, and it makes rest feel like a problem rather than a remedy. This feeling has roots that run deeper than a full schedule or a season filled with demands.

In this, Jesus calls us to Himself:

“Come to me, all you who are weary and burdened, and I will give you rest.” – Matthew 11:28, NIV

The Mixed Signals Society Sends About Rest

Today’s culture suggests that rest is something you arrive at only after you have finished everything else. It is the mindset that says you rest once the work is done and the goals are met. It is a message that rings the bell of having to prove you deserve a break.

For those already depleted, this list never ends, which means rest never quite comes. The result is a balancing act where the body is trying to slow down, and the mind is running a constant argument of why stopping is not an option.

The outcome of this internal battle is a low-grade shame that follows anytime there is a moment of stillness. It is a persistent feeling that a person should be doing something more useful than breathing. And underneath all of this is a set of competing values between the belief that productivity equals worth and the belief that stopping means you are somehow less.

For many people, this belief did not begin in adulthood. It was shaped early on in households where rest was earned, where sitting still meant you were not contributing, and where being busy was treated as proof of being responsible. Over time, this conditioning deepens. As responsibilities increase with age, the pattern becomes so familiar that rest feels foreign, and any pause has to be justified before it can be accepted.

God tells us that rest and stillness are important:

He says, “Be still, and know that I am God; I will be exalted among the nations, I will be exalted in the earth.” – Psalm 46:10, NIV

How Emotional Burnout Reshapes the Way You Experience Rest

When the nervous system operates under this prolonged pressure, urgency becomes the normal setting. This makes slowing down feel like a threat rather than a restorative action. Stillness becomes an unfamiliar territory for people experiencing high levels of chronic stress.

These individuals tend to have increased anxiety as they attempt to rest. Their system has adapted to a high state of alert, and when they step out of that, there is discomfort instead of peace. These individuals are unable to tolerate idleness, which is more common than most of us realize.

Christian counselors recognize that the inability to tolerate idleness is not failure or lack of discipline. It is a physiological and psychological response to the overwhelming busyness of carrying too much for too long. This response is going to require something more intentional than just a weekend away to unwind and refresh.

It calls for a deeper awareness of how the body has learned to associate stillness with danger and how the mind has been trained to equate doing nothing with falling behind. Without addressing this deeper pattern, even the most well-intended attempts at rest will feel incomplete or unsettling rather than restorative.

God’s heart for us is renewal and restoration:

…but those who hope in the LORD will renew their strength. They will soar on wings like eagles; they will run and not grow weary; they will walk and not be faint. – Isaiah 40:31, NIV

The Spiritual Layer of Emotional Burnout

Believers face a challenge with rest that carries a spiritual weight often overlooked. Faith communities celebrate dedication, service, and sacrifice. These values can generate competing demands and make it difficult to separate devotion from depletion. This could lead to a distorted understanding of what faithfulness actually asks.

God does not speak of rest as self-indulgence or a lack of trust. Doing less is not an indication of spiritual irresponsibility. These things are part of being a good steward of the body that God has given us.

When emotional burnout goes unaddressed within this context of faith, there is an added layer of weight in feeling as though they have let God down. Christian counselors emphasize that for those who serve in ministry, caregiving, or other high-demand callings, rest is not an absence of faithfulness. They encourage the understanding that rest is a rhythm that God established in the beginning of creation.

Then, because so many people were coming and going that they did not even have a chance to eat, he said to them, “Come with me by yourselves to a quiet place and get some rest.” – Mark 6:31, NIV

What It Looks Like to Rest Toward Healing

After a prolonged period of depletion, reclaiming rest is not about doing less. To fully rest after this type of weariness requires the individual to unlearn the beliefs that made rest feel unsafe. It is a willingness to examine the idea of value being tied to output or that productivity is proof of faithfulness. Rest in its most genuine form goes beyond sleep and includes emotional safety, relational connection, physical recovery, and spiritual nourishment.

This may look like learning to sit in stillness without immediately reaching for a task. It may involve allowing yourself to say no without feeling the need to explain. It is recognizing that fatigue is not laziness, but the body communicating a real and valid need that has gone unmet for too long. Reclaiming rest means permitting yourself to be present in your own life without the pressure of producing something in return.

Christian counselors are trained to help individuals identify which layers of rest have been missing and how to build rhythms that are sustainable and rooted in theology and grounded in the body and soul. This journey to genuine wholeness does not happen in a single decisive moment. It requires deliberate choices to stop, receive, and trust God in an act of deep faith toward long-lasting healing.

There remains, then, a Sabbath-rest for the people of God; for anyone who enters God’s rest also rests from their own works, just as God did from his. – Hebrews 4:9-10, NIV

Finding Freedom From Emotional Burnout

If rest feels wrong, you’re not alone. It’s not a sign of weakness or evidence of spiritual failure, but rather it is a result of carrying more than you should for longer than your body can sustain. The goal of rest after being depleted for so long is not to feel shame. It is to understand why stopping feels difficult and to find a path back to the rest that restores, instead of merely pausing.

God did not design us to run ourselves into the ground, even in the service of doing good. We were designed to rest after work. It is not a reward for doing something good. Choosing to understand the goodness of rest in God’s plan is a courageous step that leads to long-lasting wholeness.

If you or a loved one is navigating emotional exhaustion and finds it difficult to slow down, reach out to our reception team. They can connect you with the right person to help you navigate the balance between rest and getting everything done.

item.title: Christian-Based Counseling in Texas: Keys to Success
item.description:
Everyone strives for success, at least in one area of their lives or another, and Christian-based counseling in Texas can help. Some might consider success to be measured by the numbers in their bank account, and some might say that they’ll be a success when they hit a certain number of friends or followers on social media.

Others strive for prestige or social status in their community, aspiring to be a member of a certain social circle or club. Christians or religious people might define success differently, saying true success comes from laying down your life for others or following a preset career path in ministry.

No matter how you define success, chances are great that you’re striving for it. You may even be frustrated at the elusive nature of your goals. Success, even if it seems out of your grasp, is achievable if you embrace a few key concepts. While circumstances and opportunities vary, these principles consistently increase the likelihood of meaningful success.

Curiosity Leads to Success

Curiosity is not always celebrated in our culture. Think of all the mischief Curious George got into just because of his curiosity. The curious neighbor is often portrayed as the local gossip in popular media, and kids are sometimes told not to ask so many questions when parents don’t want to talk about a subject.

While this seems to be the cultural narrative, viewing curiosity in a negative way is damaging. Curiosity is what leads to knowledge, new experiences, and eventually, success.

Children are naturally curious. They love to explore new places and try new things. Unfortunately, adulthood has a way of stymying that curiosity in most people. But when you allow yourself to stay curious into adulthood, you permit yourself to learn. That mindset shift can change everything in your life. Curious people ask better questions, notice opportunities that others might overlook, and are far more willing to try new things, even if it means risking failure.

Curiosity pushes you to grow and explore because your desire to understand is so overwhelming that it compels you to learn. This mindset turns you from being a stymied passive bystander into an active, engaged participant in your own life.

Humility Leads to Success

Humility is another important element on the road to success. Humility is often associated with relational success, but it also plays a part in being successful in other areas of your life as well. How does being humble affect your success in business, ministry, and education, outside of its relational value?

Being humble leads to asking questions. Curiosity creates the desire to learn, but humility is what allows you to admit that you still need to. If you already think you know it all, you’re not as likely to succumb to your own curiosity. You won’t ask questions or try to learn from others because your pride tells you that you don’t need to.

If you’re full of pride, you’re also less likely to take constructive criticism. Everyone, even those with mounds of experience and skill, can make mistakes. When these inevitable mistakes happen, you can either acknowledge them and accept the occasional correction or you can blame others or circumstances. When you don’t own up to your mistakes, you miss an opportunity to grow. Not only is it a part of the growth process, but humility is a vital part of the formula for success.

Discipline Leads to Success

Being curious and humble is necessary, but if you aren’t able to sustain them, they’ll do you little good. Discipline, or perhaps another way of thinking of it, consistency, is also a key element to success.

Being disciplined requires you to learn how to live in the uncomfortable. In a society that values comfort with pillow-top beds and instant microwavable meals, it can be off-putting to live without comforts. But if you want to succeed in life, you have to learn how to survive and eventually thrive when you would rather leave or change your situation.

When you consistently put one foot in front of the other, systematically going through the steps that will lead to success, you will eventually see progress. The unfortunate reality is that many people with great ability and skill falter because they’re not disciplined enough to stay the course when the path becomes uncomfortable.

Biblical Advice

The Bible, the ultimate authority for guiding believers, agrees with the value of curiosity, humility, and discipline.

Scripture implores you to seek understanding and wisdom. In other words, the Bible tells you to be curious. Proverbs 25 says, “It is the glory of God to conceal a matter; to search out a matter is the glory of kings.” (Proverbs 25:2, NIV)

This verse eloquently discusses the profound tension that exists between the mystery of the universe and the human drive to understand it. There are aspects of existence and complexities of the universe that provide you with the why behind your curiosity.

God’s glory to conceal acknowledges that these truths remain intentionally complex or hidden. But conversely, the glory of kings is where you come in. The glory lies in the diligent labor of investigating your world. This Scripture suggests that one of the highest human achievements is to peel back those unknown layers of obscurity through research and analysis.

This curiosity and pursuit of knowledge are honorable to God and are God-given traits. He doesn’t flinch at our questions or discourage us from knowledge. He invites us to seek Him instead, and this is the source of real wisdom.

Humility, too, is championed and provides a central theme throughout the Bible. James 4:10 reminds us that if you humble yourself before the Lord, He will lift you up. True success in God’s eyes isn’t found in pride or in self-promotion. It’s the recognition that you’re dependent on Him and that you’re willing to learn from others.

In 1 Corinthians 9:24-27, Paul compares the Christian life to a race that requires training and perseverance. In other words, discipline. Success, like the Christian life, isn’t achieved overnight but requires consistency and a willingness to stay committed even when it’s difficult and even when it’s uncomfortable.

Different Goals, Same Principles

While the principles of curiosity, humility, and discipline are universal, the success they produce can look different depending on your focus. Worldly success is often centered on the accumulation of wealth, status, or influence. It’s a destination-based success.

Biblical success is measured in the transformation of your heart and defines who you are. It looks even more closely at who you are becoming and who you belong to. It’s valued in stewardship. It is not in what you have but how you’re using what you’ve already been given.

Despite these different finish lines, the mechanics of the race remain identical. The same curiosity a CEO uses to innovate a project is the curiosity a believer uses to study the depths of Scripture. The same discipline an athlete uses to train for a marathon is the discipline a person uses to maintain a consistent prayer life or to break an ingrained habit.

God has given us a powerful toolkit that helps us live successfully both in our relationship with him and the world around us.

Christian-Based Counseling in Texas: Therapy Supports Success

True success is the integration of your outward actions with your internal dialogue. It’s the realization that “searching out a matter” includes searching out the why behind your anxiety or understanding why you can’t seem to overcome a certain behavior.

Therapy can be a useful tool to help you achieve success, both in worldly and spiritual terms. When you peel back the layers of your own life, you are using your curiosity to drive success. In therapy, you will learn how to develop a sense of curiosity and humility and how to be consistent, even when uncomfortable.

Call our office to discuss how Christian-based counseling in Texas can help you find your own keys to success.

item.title: Signs of Depression in Children We Often Ignore and How to Intervene
item.description:
Every parent will tell you that children do and say unexpected things. It’s not unusual for kids to have unpredictable mood swings occasionally, develop sudden, unexpected quirks seemingly out of nowhere, or have unique preferences when it comes to their daily routine.

Reacting to these things rationally can be challenging, but most often they are harmless and amusing. However, there are certain childhood behaviors that go overlooked by parents and teachers alike, which point to something more serious happening. These are signs of depression in children.

More Than Sadness

Unfortunately, children can experience depression. It happens more often than people realize, and often affects children more deeply than they can express. Unlike sadness, depression is not a passing emotion. It cannot be fixed by a trip to the toy shop or an extra hour of screen time. Depression in children, just as with adults, is not a mood; it is a mental state that persists until it is recognized and treated.

Childhood depression is almost always linked to the following experiences:

  • A death in the family or a major life change
  • Bullying or social problems
  • Learning difficulties or academic pressures
  • Conflict and stress at home
  • Abuse and adverse childhood experiences
  • Ongoing illness or disability
  • Genetics that predispose them to mental health challenges

There could be a combination of these reasons, or a unique situation that triggers depression in a child. There might be an underlying mood disorder or condition that requires long-term treatment, or the child might benefit from play therapy or mental health support. Only when you notice the signs of depression in children can you begin to intervene and prescribe treatment for them.

Common Signs of Depression in Children and How You Can Help

Depression affects a person’s feelings, mind, and body. The signs of depression in children, therefore, are shown in their emotions, in their habits and behaviors, and in their bodies. It’s easy to overlook these symptoms because they often blend with the typical growth patterns of many kids. Keep in mind that “all behavior has meaning” and can tell you something about your child if you are paying attention.

The best you can do as a parent is to take note of any behaviors or physical symptoms that seem unusual. Speak with a doctor or mental health expert if something is persistent, extreme, or concerning to you.

Loss of Interest in Hobbies

One of the first signs of depression in children is when they suddenly become disinterested in the things they used to enjoy. They might spend more time alone, do less of the things they used to love doing, and stop participating in social events. Their teacher might tell you that they have become withdrawn in class when they used to be an active participant.

They mustn’t feel forced to reconnect with friends or to engage more socially, as this will likely make them withdraw even more. As much as possible, avoid putting them in the spotlight when talking with them. Gently invite them into activities, and when you talk with them, get down on their level.

Children withdraw to feel safe, and they will only open up if they know you won’t threaten to dismantle their emotional safe space. Often, the more that you can have this conversation come up with a child in a “natural, organic, unforced manner, the more effective it will be. This can take some strategy on your part when bringing it up, but it is worth the effort.

Emotional Outbursts

Many children have temper tantrums and the occasional angry outburst. Children instinctively regulate their emotions differently from adults. However, the one thing both kids and adults have in common is how they hide their most vulnerable emotions behind anger.

Rather than open up about what is disturbing them, they will become irritable, guarded, and angry if pushed. While you need to intervene with their angry outbursts, you must consider what is behind them, particularly if your child was never as irritable or angry before.

This is another conversation that may take some strategizing on your part to bring it up casually and thoughtfully without as many pitfalls and defensiveness on their part (and yours!). A key here is PATIENCE. Make sure you are calm first before proceeding.

It’s clear that they are dysregulated and unhappy, so scolding and punishment will only make things worse. Try to avoid minimizing their emotions by saying things like “You’re fine.” Rather, show them that you see their struggle and still love them. People of any age will only open up when they feel safe and seen. The fastest way to make a safe space for someone is to reduce criticism and make predictable routines.

Talking Negatively About Themselves

Sometimes you need to listen for signs of depression in children. They sound like “I’ll never be able to do this,” or “I’m a bad kid, and no one wants to be my friend.” These statements are glimpses into their fears and doubts. Unfortunately, if you hear things like this and don’t challenge them, these thoughts become foundational truths for your kid and determine their self-esteem for years to come.

You must intervene gently. Always acknowledge how they feel before you affirm them, or else they will feel dismissed. You can say something like, “You don’t feel good enough for your friends, huh?” before telling them that they are.

They need a model for self-compassion, so show them what it looks like. “I also feel like I’m not good enough sometimes. I remind myself that I am, even if I don’t feel like it.” Then, shine some good vibes on them by saying, “That’s sure not how I see you. Tell me more about how you see yourself.”

Struggles Concentrating

Children spend the majority of their lives in school, and so this is naturally the most common place for signs of depression to appear. Their grades might start sliding, their attendance in class declining, and their teachers might start raising concerns. This is especially a red flag if they had never struggled academically before.

You are not alone as you confront depression in your child. Hopefully, your child’s teacher cares enough to help. Together, you can outline some ways to help your child at home and at school. You might have to reduce the pressure you are putting on them to succeed, and change your tactic to be more hands-on with homework.

The teacher might have ideas on how to help with keeping them organized and focused on the work so that they don’t fall any further behind. Even if you don’t really see it this way, it’s important that you let your child know that while you want them to always do their best academically, there are more important things than making straight A’s. This includes their happiness and well-being.

Their grades can be brought back up, but addressing their mental health struggles should take priority, for now. Most children will know if their parents or caregiver are just trying to hide their disappointment, which can be toxic. Talking about it with them will help clear the air and avoid the unspoken, unaddressed shame that the child will often already be feeling.

Depression doesn’t always show up in a child’s behavior at home and school. More often than not, these signs of depression in children appear with physical symptoms and changes in routine. These are easy to ignore because kids often have physical symptoms of one kind or another, and many kids struggle with ordinary routines.

Changes in Appetite

Some kids really struggle with eating. They might prefer certain foods or eat the same meal repetitively. Most of these habits are ordinary, even when they are annoying. However, when there are big changes in the way your child eats, you should pay attention.

Just like with adults, kids cope with depression by eating more, craving sugar, or going off food entirely. If they are struggling to eat, you can help by offering them their favorite foods more frequently, and if they are overeating, reduce the snacks and junk food as much as possible. If the struggles persist for more than a month, consult a pediatrician to rule out any medical issues.

Changes in Sleep Routine

Many kids struggle with sleep at some point. Whether it’s throwing a tantrum at bedtime or taking a million years to get ready in the morning, kids have a love-hate relationship with sleep. However, count it as a warning sign when they consistently have issues falling asleep or waking up, to the point that it affects their day and drains their energy.

Regardless of what they say or do, children thrive on routine and consistency. You can create a calming bedtime routine by reducing screen time an hour before bed and turning the lights down low in their bedroom. Consider replacing screen time with other activities like reading or drawing before bedtime.

In case it comes up, keep in mind that trading the iPad for the phone does not count as “adjusting screen time.” Adjust the temperature if possible, speak in calming voices, and rehearse nightly routines, such as brushing teeth and saying prayers. These things will not target depression, but they help children get the right amount of sleep by keeping routines, which greatly reduces the effects of depression.

If you suspect that your child is dealing with depression, please reach out. Our reception team can connect you with me or another counselor who can provide support to you as an individual, to your child, or to your family group. Please contact our online reception team or consult our online directory for more information.

item.title: Healthy Mind: 6 Life Changes That Are Also Good for the Soul
item.description:
When identifying what makes for a healthy mind, we could look to any number of psychological theories for an answer. However, each theory varies in what it believes are the core components of what makes one’s mind healthy. Some theories focus on emotional awareness, while others focus more on flexibility of thinking.

Before modern psychological theories were created, the Bible spoke about how to have a healthy mind. Philippians 4:8 tells us to think about things that are honorable, just, pure, and lovely. If we aren’t used to focusing our mind on such things, it takes time to create these habits that lead to a healthier mind. Changing ways that we think and behave can be especially difficult when some of the unhealthy habits we currently possess have been with us since we were young.

Throughout our lifetime, we can learn and incorporate unhealthy habits without even being aware. Habits such as negativity, people-pleasing, distrust of others, and perfectionism (to name a few) can have an unfavorable impact on how we see ourselves, other people, and the world around us. If we continue in these unhealthy habits for long periods of time, it can take a toll on our mental health and lead to issues such as depression and anxiety.

The Nature of Creating Healthy Habits

Take a moment to think back to a time when you tried to do something new that would benefit your life. Perhaps you tried eating healthier or exercising more regularly. Maybe you decided to spend less money and to put more money away for a rainy day. Maybe you tried to be less critical in a relationship and improve communication. Were you successful in forming new ways of behaving? If so, how long did it take before the new behaviors seemed automatic?

Researchers Lally, van Jaarsveld, Potts, and Wardle conducted a study in 2009, concluding that it usually takes around sixty-six days before a new habit feels automatic. However, the time to create the new habit can vary widely (18-254 days) based on the complexity of the desired behavior, personal motivation, and the surrounding circumstances in which the person is trying to create the habit.

The good news is that the researchers also found that slipping up and missing a single day does not significantly harm the overall long-term success of creating a healthy habit (Lally et al.). In this article, we will look at six life changes that you can turn into habits that will contribute to a healthier mind as well as positively increase how you feel about yourself and others.

Remember that adopting new behaviors can be challenging, so you may want to pick one new habit to start at a time. Be kind and forgiving to yourself if you mess up because, even if you must start the new behavior again, it just reinforces to the mind that it’s worth doing.

Cultivate hope and optimism
The Cambridge English Dictionary defines optimism as “the quality of being full of hope and emphasizing the good parts of a situation, or a belief that something good will happen.” We have numerous ways of looking at the world with hopeful expectations. As a child, did you ever throw a penny into a wishing well, hoping the wish would come true? How about wishing upon a star or making a wish while blowing out birthday cake candles?

Some people believe that hope and optimism are lost once you become an adult with serious responsibilities. With this outlook, individuals can get into a habit of complaining about everything. Complaining can be contagious but hope and optimism can be contagious too. Researchers have found that both optimism and hope are related to greater happiness (Snyder, 2002; Carver & Scheier, 2014).

Optimism is often paired with hope, but they are not the same thing. Optimism is a general outlook that good rather than bad things will happen, while hope tends to be focused on something specific. Hope focused on a specific goal may make you more likely to succeed. This is what is called a self-fulfilling prophecy.

The way you think can drive your behavior to the point of success or defeat, depending on whether your thoughts are positive or negative. The cycle then begins. The more optimistic and hopeful you are, the more success you may see. This, in turn, can make a person more optimistic and hopeful in the future. The great thing about optimism and hope is that anyone can learn these skills by becoming more aware and incorporating them into their daily life.

Simple Ways to Practice Hope and Optimism

  • Look up quotes from inspiring people that foster a sense of optimism and hope. Here are some of my favorites:

“When the world says give up, hope whispers, try it one more time.” – H. Jackson Brown, Jr.

“Keep your face to the sunshine, and you cannot see the shadows.” – Helen Keller

“Whether you think you can, or you think you can’t, you’re right.” – Henry Ford

  • Every day for a week, catch yourself when you are complaining. Try to take the circumstances you are complaining about and find something positive about it.
  • Name a source of inspiration you have. It could be a person or something that provides a sense of purpose. Think about why you find them/it inspiring. Could you be someone else’s source of inspiration?

Practicing gratitude
Consider this quote from Joyce Meyer: “I’m not where I want to be, but thank God I’m not where I used to be.” This quote shows that we don’t have to have it all together to be thankful for the progress we have made.

Gratitude in our everyday lives helps us to value what we have and decrease the focus on what we don’t have. Learning to increase gratitude helps us to appreciate and savor those everyday events and experiences and can also increase satisfaction in relationships.

How do we begin to increase gratitude in our lives? Gratitude is not just something we identify at Thanksgiving or Christmas but needs to be a habit that we incorporate daily to reap the benefits. We all have things that we wish were different in our lives, but we also have numerous things for which we can be thankful.

Taking time to identify the small things that we are blessed with can help to begin a pattern of gratitude. Gratitude can also be displayed in how we appreciate others. When was the last time you thanked someone for something small that they did? Creating this habit of thanking people close to you for all the small things they do can help to develop a habit of gratitude.

Plus, you get the added benefit of having a more positive relationship with that person. Overall, gratitude is one of the easiest life changes that a person can incorporate and has the biggest social and personal payoff, contributing to a healthier mind.

Simple Ways to Practice Gratitude

  • Write a thank-you note to someone who has made a difference in your life. Explain to them what they have done and what this means to you.
  • Every day for a week, write down three things that happened during the day for which you are thankful.
  • Take a walk outside. Notice different things that you see, hear, smell, and touch. As you walk, name the things in your life for which you are grateful.

Develop an attitude of curiosity
The Cambridge English Dictionary defines Curiosity as “An eager wish or desire to acquire new information or investigate strange things.” When we think about curiosity, we might think of a child learning about the world around them or how researchers come to achieve scientific breakthroughs. However, developing an attitude of curiosity about the people that we interact with every day can help decrease conflict and develop an increased level of empathy.

We each have our own interpretations of life and how the world around us works. This is called our perspective. Our perspective is determined by many things. Our genetics, the temperament we are born with, our culture, and the experiences we have throughout life can all influence perspective.

A large part of our perspective develops during the early years of life and can be highly impacted by our early caregiving relationships. Our perspective is made up of good experiences, bad experiences, and everything in-between.

Often, we misinterpret a situation because we judge the circumstances by our own perspectives. Our brains are wired to scan for information we are familiar with that might explain what is going on in any given circumstance. The researchers at the HeartMath Institute (2019) found that we have emotional responses to our perceptions of events.

These emotional responses usually lead us to negatively judge people and situations. When we are hurt by others in those situations, we can become distrustful and feel as though we have to protect ourselves. These trust issues can spread and become part of our overall perspective of people. We put up emotional walls and begin to judge the intentions of others quickly, which leads to miscommunication and increased conflict.

It causes hurt to be continually passed on. To approach a situation without judgment takes practice and a desire to be curious about how others might view things differently than yourself. This is called “perspective taking.” This can be a challenge, since we never really know what others are thinking unless they tell us.

However, practicing perspective taking with an attitude of curiosity toward others can help cultivate a healthy mind. Having an attitude of curiosity can help decrease personal frustration, thus decreasing health-damaging cortisol levels. An attitude of curiosity can also help increase patience in yourself and strengthen your relationships.

Simple Ways to Practice Curiosity

  • Analyze the way you view others’ intentions. Are you always thinking that people are out to harm you?
  • Pick a person with whom you don’t agree on something. Try to describe the reasons why that person may think differently than you.
  • The next time you interact with someone from a different culture or geographic location than your own, ask them about their favorite thing about their culture or the place they are from.

Develop a Sense of Humor
What people find humorous can vary from person to person based on their perspective. But the fact is, people like to laugh and be entertained. After all, laughter increases social bonding and is contagious, spreading from person to person to lighten the mood. As we look around our world, we find that a lot of time, money, and effort are spent creating ways to make people laugh, such as through music, movies, and art.

There is something positive that happens in our brains when we experience humor. According to researchers at Harvard University (2010), the surprising characteristic of a joke causes parts of your brain to search for a recognizable pattern. When the punchline comes, the brain shifts from trying to process information to looking for an emotional response.

During this process, your brain releases chemicals called neurotransmitters that make you feel good. So, having a good, hearty laugh can result in positive results for the body. Laughter has been found to relieve tension, decrease pain and stress, enhance the experience of pleasure, boost the immune system, and help reduce the risk of heart attack and stroke (Harvard University). Laughter really is the best medicine.

Life can be unpredictable, not fair, and downright out of control at times. The difficulty lies in being able to laugh about a mistake we make, when a mishap occurs, or when life just isn’t rolling out how we expect. We usually can’t reverse what happens to us and, if we are alive and learning the lessons of life, we are going to make mistakes.

Humor can be a valuable way of coping when things do not go as expected. Being able to find humor in a tough situation can help lessen the negative impact that it has on your mood and decrease your stress.

Simple Ways to Practice Humor

  • The next time you are feeling down, set aside some time to watch a funny movie or watch your favorite comedian.
  • Describe a really awkward past moment in your life. Can you laugh about this today?
  • If aliens were to abduct you, describe three silly things you do that would make them send you back.
  • Next time you are struggling, exaggerate about how things might be worse. Coming up with silly ways that a situation could have gone can help you find some humor in your current circumstance.

Experience pleasure in a healthy way
Researchers have found that pleasure is an important part of healthy psychological functioning and well-being (Berridge & Kringelbach, 2015). In fact, anhedonia, which is a symptom of depression, is when a person has difficulty finding pleasure in anything they experience. You can imagine how this would cause psychological functioning to decrease.

On the other hand, some experiences of pleasure can lead to addictive behavior. Most people might agree that eating indulgent foods, winning money at a slot machine, or playing a thrilling video game can create pleasurable experiences, but too much of anything can become excessive and unhealthy.

When examining what things bring pleasure, people also find that helping a friend, solving a problem, creating something artistic, meeting a goal, appreciating nature, and engaging in calming prayer or worship also provide pleasurable experiences. Some people might even say that these latter kinds of pleasures are more valuable overall since they tend to be more lasting (Heathwood, 2013).

When pursued with a healthy balance, pleasure brings about appreciation, playfulness, sensuality, spontaneity, and a healthy focus on self-care (Huta, 2014). In fact, healthy pleasure is essential for self-care and can increase feelings of joy, comfort, and relaxation.

There is a skill used in psychology, created by Fred Bryant, called savoring that helps to enhance an appreciation for pleasure and to regulate emotional states. The skill of savoring is more than just feeling and enjoying pleasure. Savoring requires a person to put forth conscious, mindful awareness.

This allows a person to fully soak in and prolong an experience while appreciating the positive emotions they feel. Savoring can be used to experience pleasure related to things in the past, present, or future. The savoring of pleasurable experiences helps to combat negative emotions, which can lead to depression and anxiety.

Simple Ways to Practice Pleasure

  • Choose something new to try that you have never done before. Examples could be trying a new and strange type of food, engaging in a type of sport you have never tried, or researching a topic of interest that you know nothing about.
  • List at least three things you think are beautiful. Describe them and really focus on detail.
  • Name something that you used to love as a kid. Do it again, no matter how silly it may seem. If you can’t do it, then imagine what it was like when you were a kid. Remember how it made you feel.
  • Is there something pleasurable that you are doing in excess that is creating problems in your life? Create a plan about how you could use more moderation.

Create positive social interactions
Have you ever had a bad day that was completely turned around by someone just noticing you and being nice? How does it make you feel when someone walking by smiles and says, “Good morning?” Have you ever had someone pay for your order at a drive-thru? These are small behaviors that work reciprocally. This means that the receiver and the giver of the kindness both benefit.

Performing small acts, like opening the door for someone, smiling, being friendly to the person waiting on you in a store, and telling someone to have a nice day, are some of the easiest ways to change your mood. Even better, it begins to change the mood of the people around you, creating a more positive environment.

According to the Mental Health Foundation (2019), depression and anxiety are the most common mental health issues. Even though these issues are common, when we are experiencing depression or anxiety, we often think we are the only ones who feels this way. People that you interact with every day may also be feeling depressed and/or anxious. We don’t know who they are because we have all gotten good at hiding how we really feel.

Many people around us are lonely, grieving, scared, or feel forgotten. You may be feeling that way right now. Simply smiling and being kind to someone can make them feel seen, valued, and at ease.

At the same time, you can feel seen, valued, and at ease when the person reciprocates with a warm response. Incorporating positive social interactions into your everyday life can create an atmosphere of compassion and generosity, as well as help combat feelings of depression and anxiety.

Simple Ways to Practice Positive Social Interactions 

  • Do you have difficulty asking for help when you need it? How does it feel when you help someone? Find something small that you need help with and ask someone to help you. When the task is done, reflect on how it made you feel and how you think the other person felt.
  • In the morning, every day for a week, smile and say good morning to passers-by. What kind of reactions did you get? Do you think it helped increase your mood?
  • Try doing a random act of kindness for someone. Examples could be writing an encouraging message for someone in the office who may get overlooked for what they do. You could let someone with fewer groceries go in front of you in line at the store, pay for someone’s morning coffee, or when you ask someone how they are, really listen.

Where to Find Help

Some life changes are easier than others to incorporate and make into habits. When unhealthy habits become rooted in everyday life and are leading to issues such as depression, anxiety, and conflict in relationships, extra help is needed to make life changes.

Contacting our office at Texas Christian Counseling can help connect you to Christian counselors who can support and guide you in creating positive life changes that align with your values while also improving the health of your mind and the quality of your relationships.

item.title: Working Through Church Hurt: Finding Healing and Hope
item.description:
Jesus said to His disciples, “In this world you will have trouble. But take heart! I have overcome the world.” (John 16:33, NIV) Being a disciple of Jesus comes with its fair share of struggles, but the encouragement is that Jesus has triumphed over the worst this world could do to us. One particularly difficult challenge is when the source of trouble comes not from the world out there, but from God’s own people. Church hurt is a reality that many have experienced.

Church Hurt: A Painful Reality

The community of God’s people is meant to be a different sort of community. It is composed of people who are dealing with their own struggles, but this is a community being changed and transformed into the likeness of the Son (2 Corinthians 3:18), and it is a community that is led by God’s own Spirit (Galatians 5:16-26; Romans 8:5-17). It is supposed to be a place of encouragement, refuge, and growth in Christ.

All of this is what the church, the community of God’s people, is supposed to be. However, it is also true that in many ways and across many centuries, the church has also been a source of deep pain. This is true for people in the church and those outside of it. For those who can be considered insiders because they also believe in Jesus as Lord, church hurt can cause emotional and spiritual damage and leave lasting scars that require healing and restoration.

What is church hurt? Church hurt can be understood as the relational, spiritual, physical, and emotional wounds that are caused in the context of a church community. This kind of hurt can be the result of betrayals of trust, feeling excluded, abuse of authority, hypocrisy, gossip, or judgmental attitudes through the words, actions, or postures of fellow congregants, leaders, or the culture within that community and other communities around it.

Church hurt thus occurs when the community that is meant to be a signpost and reflection of Christ’s love becomes a place of deep wounding. Church hurt can happen in subtle ways that chip away at the foundations of relationships and in abrupt and traumatic ways as well. Something like feeling dismissed, overlooked, or unvalued can lead to church hurt, just as experiencing bullying, manipulation, or spiritual abuse can.

The pain caused by these actions is all too real. Often, the result is that the person who was hurt may become disillusioned with their faith altogether. They can begin to mistrust leadership or lose their sense of connection to the body of Christ.

The Various Paths of Church Hurt

Church hurt can come about in several ways. When Jesus was asked why He ate and spent time with unsavory characters, He responded, saying, “It is not the healthy who need a doctor, but the sick. I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners.” (Mark 2:17, NIV) One of the main reasons why church hurt occurs is because churches are essentially hospitals full of desperately sick people in need of a savior. Church is a community of imperfect people.

The church is a community of people who have been rescued from themselves through Christ and given new lives empowered by the Holy Spirit (Colossians 3:1-17; Ephesians 2:1-10; Romans 8).

Believers are saved by the unmerited favor of God and called to a new way of life. However, Christians are still human, struggling with old patterns of sin and harmful behaviors. These are to be put to death, and that highlights the ongoing challenge that they are for believers.

Misuse of authority is a major cause of church hurt. That includes leaders behaving in domineering, abusive, and controlling ways that betray trust and misrepresent Jesus. Abuse can be physical, sexual, financial, emotional, and spiritual in nature. Whatever form it takes, it’s a leader misusing their position and damaging others along the way.

Relationships can be deeply damaged in the church because of harsh judgment and gossip. Divisive words spoken outright or behind people’s backs can erode the cohesion of a church community, and being judgmental can demean others and leave them feeling isolated.

There is a vast difference between speaking truth to one another in love (Ephesians 4:11-16) and holding each other accountable and standing in haughty judgment of one another (Galatians 6:1-10).

Apart from gossip and judgment, another source of church hurt is unmet expectations. It is right to expect great things from the community of God’s people. However, hurt can arise when one expects the community to meet every spiritual, physical, and emotional need perfectly.

In  the church, there will be a lot of give and take, a lot of learning and growing together. That is one reason Scripture calls us to bear with and forgive each other (Colossians 3:12-14; Ephesians 4:32).

Another common source of church hurt is when there are conflicts originating in cultural differences or doctrinal issues. As a collective of people from every nation, people, and tribe, and as the church is made up of people from every walk of life, there will be differences. These can be in worship styles, theological emphases, or church practices. When these differences are handled poorly or insensitively, things can escalate, and people can wound each other deeply.

Church hurt can be the result of intentional as well as unintentional actions, behaviors, attitudes, and postures that individuals or communities take. These can be the source of lasting pain, especially when they go unrecognized and aren’t dealt with wisely, in humility and love. The issue of distributing aid among widows threatened the early church, and thankfully, the disciples dealt wisely and swiftly with the concerns (Acts 6:1-7).

The reality of church hurt is an ever-present one. The community of God’s people needs to continuously rely on the Lord’s grace and wisdom as they pursue genuine accountability and seek restoration of what is broken.

How Church Hurt Impacts Individuals and the Community

The community of God’s people is often described as a body (Ephesians 4:1-16; 1 Corinthians 12; Colossians 3:15). That’s one reason why Paul writes that there shouldn’t be division in the body, and instead “its parts should have equal concern for each other. If one part suffers, every part suffers with it; if one part is honored, every part rejoices with it.” (1 Corinthians 12:25-26, NIV) Christians often forget that they are part of Christ’s body along with others.

For individual believers, church hurt can have the effect of a loss of trust in spiritual leadership. There are probably too many stories that have been told describing the aftermath of a betrayal by a pastor or other church leader. There may be feelings of confusion, bitterness, and anger that result from church hurt. This can lead to emotional withdrawal or isolation if one doesn’t have space to process things with the community.

Another devastating result of church hurt is that it can result in questioning God’s goodness and even one’s own faith. If a church leader gaslights a congregant, for instance, the congregant may believe they are to blame and that their faith is defective in some way. It can take years to overcome this kind of damage. Some people have left the church altogether because of the deep spiritual wounds they’ve experienced.

The community is also affected by church hurt in various ways. A church may struggle to thrive in the wake of church hurt, especially if matters aren’t dealt with honestly. A culture of suspicion, fear, or division can take root and shape how people interact with one another.

If the community hardens its heart toward a particular individual, or if an individual or group of individuals is the source of hurt for the broader community, that can affect the dynamics of the community. Church hurt can weaken unity and damage the effective witness of Christ’s body. A community may struggle to regain its sense of self. When wounded members withdraw or leave the community, the sense of fellowship may suffer.

Finding Healing and Hope After Church Hurt

While it’s not quick or easy, restoration, healing, and hope are possible with the Lord’s help and presence. If you’ve experienced church hurt, the movement toward healing will involve intentional steps that include:

Acknowledge the pain The hurt exists, and you can name it along with the grief it’s caused before the Lord through lament.

Seek the Lord’s heart Spend time in Scripture and prayer to hear the Lord’s heart for His church. Ultimately, He is the head of the church (Ephesians 4:11-16), and He is building it (Matthew 16:18).

Humbly assess your own heart Hurt may be the result of others’ actions, but it is nonetheless wise to humbly examine if there are areas where you may need to take responsibility. This isn’t to excuse wrongdoing or victim-blame, but to ensure your own heart remains open, forgiving, and teachable. Jesus calls believers to remove the log from their own eye before addressing the speck in another’s (Matthew 7:3-5).

Forgive Forgiveness gives you freedom. It doesn’t mean forgetting or going back into unsafe situations, but it allows you to release resentment and entrust justice in the Lord’s hands (Romans 12:17-21).

Pursue healing and connection Finding healing may involve hard conversations with those you hurt or those who hurt you, where this is appropriate and safe. Consider re-engaging with a church community, even if it’s a different one, because we are meant to be in community with others.

Seek support Making sense of church hurt is best done in a context with trusted mature believers or with a trained and licensed Christian counselor. Your counselor can listen, pray with you, and guide you, helping to break the power of isolation and offering perspective.

With help, you can discover renewed hope and a deeper, more resilient faith. Contact our reception team or browse our online counselor directory to process the pain from church hurt.

item.title: Dealing with Anxiety in Pregnancy, Labor, and Delivery
item.description:
The birth of a child can be a time of excitement, joy, and wonder as one experiences the miracle of life. Starting from the moment of finding out one is expecting, to hearing the heartbeat for the first time, to preparing the nursery, culminating in that moment one first sees what love between two people was able to create when the baby takes their first breath. Becoming a mom/parent truly is one of the highest blessings that is even reflected in Scripture.

Children are a heritage from the Lord, offspring a reward from him. Like arrows in the hands of a warrior are children born in one’s youth. Blessed is the man whose quiver is full of them. – Psalm 127:3-4, NIV

Anxiety and Pregnancy

However, the reality is that for most, there is some level of anxiety related to the unknowns, particularly regarding the labor and delivery aspects of becoming a parent. It is only natural for one to worry about the pain and the safety/health of not only their baby, but also the woman bearing the child. A lot of this is normal and even beneficial for most mothers, prompting them to take steps to prepare for the delivery process.

Some steps women may take in preparation are finding a provider they feel comfortable with, asking questions, taking classes to learn positions and comforting measures during the labor process, reading books/listening to podcasts to know what to bring to the hospital, taking tours of the hospital to familiarize themselves with the space, and talking to other women who have been through the experience.

All of these measures are great as long as the woman understands that no matter how much research they do, questions they ask, books they read, or people they talk to, it is the norm to still feel like you aren’t prepared enough, especially when it comes to the delivery of your first child. Having a good support system to remind you of this and to continue encouraging you is crucial, especially as your due date approaches.

Unfortunately, though, there are some women who not only experience the “normal” level of worry during their pregnancy and delivery, but their anxiety reaches what we call “clinical levels.” What this means is that their anxiety is persistent and excessive to the point where it starts interfering with their daily functioning.

Clinical levels of anxiety can then turn a time in life that should be exciting and memorable into one that is daunting, overwhelming, and isolating, with women asking themselves, “Why am I not enjoying this?”

Causes of Anxiety in Pregnancy

Many factors can lead to diagnosable anxiety during pregnancy. These factors can be broken down into three categories: biological, psychological, and social/environmental.

Biological factors include:

  • A preexisting anxiety disorder or history of anxiety, depression, or other mental health conditions
  • A family history of anxiety or other mental health conditions
  • Hormonal changes that occur in pregnancy
  • High-risk pregnancy and/or pregnancy complications
  • Other medical conditions like thyroid disorders, PCOS, etc. that can affect mood and hormones
  • Medical conditions that can lead to complications in pregnancy
  • Insomnia or lack of sleep

Psychological factors include:

  • High levels of stress
  • Previous history of trauma, particularly sexual trauma
  • History of infertility, miscarriages, stillbirths
  • Previous traumatic pregnancy/birth experiences
  • Previous history of a newborn admission to the NICU (Neonatal Intensive Care Unit)

Social/Environmental factors include:

  • An unplanned/unwanted pregnancy
  • Limited social support
  • Financial stress, lack of stable housing or employment
  • Relationship/marital conflict
  • Domestic partner abuse
  • Attachment problems or strained relationships with one’s parents

Though these factors do not always lead to diagnosable anxiety during pregnancy it can put someone at higher risk. If this is the case for you, you are not alone, and there is hope. It may seem that some of these factors are out of your control; however, there are many steps you can take when it comes to this significant life event of bringing a child into the world.

Finding a mental health counselor is a great resource and means of support whether you are experiencing normal levels of worry or significant levels of anxiety during your pregnancy. Not only that, but if you are not yet pregnant but know you are at high risk, proactively seeking counseling is a great way to not only take care of yourself but also prepare yourself to be the best parent you can be for your child.

How Counseling Can Help

If you are already struggling with an anxiety disorder or other mental health condition, a counselor can help equip you with coping skills to help manage your anxiety. A counselor can also help you gain an understanding of your anxiety, including how anxiety works in your body, help you identify triggers, and provide psychoeducation about factors that may worsen your anxiety.

If you are someone who has been through significant trauma, a counselor can help you process that trauma and guide you on a path toward healing using trauma-based therapy modalities. A counselor can also help prepare you for how pregnancy and labor may trigger increased anxiety and how to manage those situations.

If you are someone who has experienced infertility, miscarriages, stillbirth, delivery trauma, or a previous newborn admission into the NICU, a counselor can help you process the grief that often comes with these experiences – grief that is not only related to the loss of a child, but also the loss of not having that smooth labor and delivery experience you had hoped for.

Often, these situations create increased fear coming into a hospital setting, and a counselor can teach you how to challenge these fears and challenge any inappropriate guilt that can also come with these experiences.

If you are someone who has an unplanned pregnancy, relationship/marital conflict, or lack of social support, a counselor can help you process your emotions regarding the unplanned pregnancy. An individual counselor can help you navigate the conflict in your relationship.

Or if your partner is open to it, a couple’s counselor could be a great resource to help equip you and your partner with communication/conflict resolution skills and be a mediator as you navigate decision-making regarding raising and caring for a child. A counselor can also help you identify ways to build your support system so that you do not feel alone during your pregnancy or delivery.

If you are someone dealing with stress or financial challenges, a counselor can help provide you with resources and stress management skills, as well as be a resource to identify possible solutions to the stressors you’re experiencing.

These are just a few of the ways a mental health counselor can help in managing anxiety in pregnancy and the delivery of a child. As a mental health counselor who also works as a labor and delivery nurse, I often see how severe anxiety can affect a woman’s delivery experience.

I am passionate about walking women through pre-pregnancy, pregnancy, labor and delivery, and postpartum stages. I love helping prepare women to take on one of the most important roles in their lives. What I have seen is that by taking the time and effort now to deal with anxiety and mental health concerns, you are, in effect, creating a significant impact not only on your children but on generations to come.
