item.title: The Same Struggle, Different Signs: Anxiety and Depression in Men and Women
item.description:
Anxiety and depression don’t look the same for everyone. If you’ve ever wondered why one person’s distress looks like constant worry while another’s looks like irritability or shutting down, you’re already noticing something researchers have been studying for decades: gender plays a meaningful role in how emotional disorders are experienced and expressed.

This isn’t about stereotypes or assumptions. It’s about biology, hormones, social conditioning, and different ways men and women are taught to cope with distress. When we understand these patterns, we get better at recognizing anxiety and depression in ourselves and in the people we care about.

Women are diagnosed more often, but that’s not the whole story

Large population studies consistently show that women are diagnosed with both anxiety and depression at higher rates than men. But this doesn’t mean women are “more emotional” or that men don’t struggle. It means:

  • Women’s symptoms tend to match what the mental health field traditionally recognizes as anxiety or depression.
  • Men’s symptoms often show up in ways that don’t immediately look like emotional distress.

So, the real story isn’t “women are more anxious or depressed.” It’s “women’s distress is easier to see, and men’s distress is easier to miss.”

Behind the Scenes: What’s Going on in the Body

Research points to several biological factors that shape how anxiety and depression show up. These internal systems don’t determine destiny, but they do influence how our nervous systems respond to stress and overwhelming emotions.

Hormonal Fluctuations: Estrogen and progesterone influence stress‑response systems, which helps explain why anxiety and depression can spike during menstrual cycles, pregnancy, and perimenopause. Testosterone appears to have a modest protective effect.

Brain circuitry differences: Studies show sex‑linked differences in how the amygdala and stress‑response systems activate.

Genetic Architecture: Women show more anxiety‑related genetic variants, and depression often co‑occurs with internalizing traits like rumination and self‑criticism.

These “under the hood” factors help explain why women often experience internalizing symptoms – and why men may be more prone to externalizing patterns.

The Roles We’re Told to Play (Social Conditioning)

Biology sets the stage, but culture directs the performance.

Women are encouraged to express emotion Talking about fear, sadness, or feelings of being overwhelmed is more socially acceptable. As a result, women’s anxiety and depression often show up in ways that are easy to name: worry, panic, sadness, withdrawal.

Men are encouraged to be stoic Admitting fear or vulnerability can feel like breaking a rule. So, men’s distress often shows up sideways: irritability, overworking, risk‑taking, or emotional avoidance.

Same underlying distress  –  different socially acceptable “costumes.”

On Stage: How These Emotions Show Up

These factors shape why what we see looks different. If you’re a child of the nineties like I am, you grew up watching Monica on Friends hide anxiety through perfectionism, over functioning, and people-pleasing. She manages stress by controlling her environment, overachieving, and trying to meet everyone’s expectations. Her anxiety looks “productive,” but it’s driver by fear of failure and self-criticism.

Contrast that with a depiction of someone like Tony Stark. He externalizes his anxiety through being a workaholic, emotional avoidance, bravado, and productivity. Instead of expressing fear or vulnerability, he doubles down on control, innovation, and performance. These characters help us recognize that anxiety isn’t always panic or fear- it can look like being overly responsible, overly accommodating, or overly busy.

We see similar patterns with depression. If you have little kids, you’ve probably gone through (or are still going through) the Frozen stage. Elsa is a great example of internalizing depression, the form more commonly seen in women. Her emotional distress turns inward: isolation, shame, fear of being a burden, and a deep sense of not belonging.

So, she withdraws from relationships, suppresses her feelings, and carries her pain alone. Men, on the other hand, tend to externalize depression. Here, grief and hopelessness can be expressed through emotional suppression, detachment, or even risk-taking. Instead of slowing down, they might throw themselves into danger, productivity, and control.

Seeing Your Performance More Clearly

Understanding these patterns isn’t about diagnosing yourself or fitting into a category. It’s about finally recognizing the ways your own “performance” on stage may have been shaped by things happening behind the scenes- biology, expectations, and the roles you were taught to play.

So, let’s slow down and look at your performance more clearly.

Get curious about how distress shows up

  • When you’re overwhelmed, do you shut down or speed up?
  • Do you get quieter, or do you get busier?
  • Do you feel everything intensely, or do you feel nothing at all?

Ask questions you may not be used to asking

Instead of “Am I anxious?” or “Am I depressed?” try asking:

  • Do I get irritable or short when I’m overwhelmed?
  • Do I feel constantly on edge, even when I might be functioning well?
  • Do I worry about being a burden or disappointing people?
  • Do I feel like I must hold everything together, so nothing falls apart?

These questions help you see what’s happening beneath the performance- the part that often gets missed.

Notice the story you were taught about emotions

Were you taught to be the strong one? The responsible one? The easy one? The one who doesn’t make waves? Or were you taught to be accommodating, pleasant, and self‑sacrificing? Those roles shape how you show distress – and how you hide it.

Pay attention to the moments when you feel out of character

Maybe you’re the dependable one, but lately you’re exhausted. Maybe you’re the calm one, but lately you’re snapping at people. Maybe you’re the high‑achiever, but lately everything feels heavy. Those shifts are often the first signs that something deeper is happening backstage.

Let this be an invitation, not a diagnosis

You don’t have to decide today whether you’re anxious or depressed. You don’t have to fit neatly into a category or have to have the “right” symptoms. You must notice what’s happening inside you – and consider that your distress might be showing up in ways you weren’t taught to recognize.

When the Curtain Falls

There’s a moment- sometimes quiet, sometimes overwhelming- when the performance stops. When the curtain falls, and you’re no longer playing the role you’ve been handed. When the audience disappears, and it’s just you, standing in the wings, feeling the weight of what you’ve been carrying.

Maybe you’ve realized you’re exhausted from holding everything together. Maybe you’ve noticed that no matter how much you achieve, it never feels like enough. Maybe you’ve caught yourself chasing a version of peace that always seems one step out of reach. Maybe you’re starting to see that the role you’ve been performing doesn’t match what’s happening inside you, and this is exactly why it matters that anxiety and depression look different in everyone.

Because if you’ve spent years looking for the “classic” symptoms, you may have missed your own. You may have dismissed irritability as stress, overworking as responsibility, numbness as burnout, people‑pleasing as personality. You may have believed you were fine simply because your distress didn’t look like the version you were taught to expect.

Seeing your performance more clearly helps you recognize what’s been happening backstage – the tension, the overwhelming stress, the emptiness, the pressure – not as personal failures, but as signals that something in you is asking to be understood. And when you reach this place, that’s the part of the story where things can finally begin to shift. When the curtain falls, that’s where the real work begins- and where real relief becomes possible.

item.title: What Does Forgiveness Mean If You Are Stuck in Trauma?
item.description:
You hear the word used in relation to healing, and you know that unforgiveness is like a poison, but what does forgiveness mean when you strip away all of the clichés and shallow advice? If it were so easy to do, then why do people struggle with it so much? Surely there are steps or stages to forgiveness, just as there are with grief or addiction?

The truth is that forgiveness is probably a lot different from the things people have said it is. Forgiveness is not a choice you make once and try to stick to. In fact, it has nothing to do with your mentality or mindset. It is about changing your relationship to the person who hurt you, or changing your life until you can face them again.

Forgiveness is something you do to release your nervous system from being stuck in trauma. As long as you are holding onto the memory of what you experienced, your nervous system is kept in survival mode. This results in using all of your physical energy to protect you from a danger that is no longer present. Forgiveness and healing go together and cannot be separated, but the path to both might be different from what you have been taught.

What does forgiveness mean?

Forgiveness happens in your body. The emotions you feel are an echo of something happening in your body. Your nervous system feels everything you do. Anxiety can feel like a tightness in your chest, sadness like a lump in your throat, anger like a heat that flushes your face, and exhaustion like a tension in your shoulders.

When you experience the emotions caused by unforgiveness, like bitterness, resentment, fury, and disbelief, your nervous system remains activated and ready to face the threat that it thinks is causing you to feel these things. You know that these events are in the past, but your nervous system never got the memo. It responds to all these memories, emotions, and triggers as if they were a present danger.

Each time you remember the person who hurt you, or the events that traumatized you, it is a signal to your nervous system that it must fight, escape, shut down temporarily, or try to figure out a way to avoid the pain. It is like being haunted by a ghost that cannot physically harm you except by the anxiety and distress its presence causes you. As long as these events are being replayed in your memories, they are a present threat to your body.

What does forgiveness mean? Forgiveness means giving your nervous system a chance to relax. It is the act of moving to a place that is not haunted by the past and getting a good night’s sleep for the first time in years.

Forgiveness only involves you

If you were waiting to forgive that person only after they made an apology, offered an olive branch, or simply acknowledged their actions, you might wait forever. You don’t need their participation to forgive them.

It’s painful to realize that they have no plans to try to salvage the relationship or take ownership of their part in what happened. When you realize that you need to move on for your own good, even if that means you will never get an apology or acknowledgment, you have begun the healing process.

Forgiveness only waits on you alone. You might not feel ready to let things go because it takes a long time to heal from injustice. Your tormentor only has enough power over you as you give them, though. Forgiveness happens in your body and according to your own timeline. What does forgiveness mean if not healing simply because you deserve to?

Healing comes before forgiveness

The most traumatic event in your life has happened, and it has altered events for good. It was unfair, it was brutal, and it caused some serious damage that will take years to recover from. Forgiving the person who did this to you does not mean that you have to overlook this damage. In fact, it is only once you begin healing the harm that was done that you can begin forgiving the one who did it. First comes healing, then comes forgiveness.

You can choose to forgive someone because you know it’s the right thing to do, and you can say all the appropriate words to formalize your decision. Forgiveness isn’t as simple as making the choice or doing the right thing, though.

You can choose to forgive them, mentally release them, and even genuinely pray for their well-being, but until your nervous system has processed the trauma and begun healing, you cannot truly forgive or forget. What does forgiveness mean? It means giving yourself the time to heal and process the trauma so that you can move on.

Releasing the Debt

Have you ever noticed how much of the language we use to talk about forgiveness mirrors the things we say about money? We say, “they owe me an apology”, or, “I would feel better if I could get some payback.” When Jesus taught his disciples how to pray, He linked forgiveness with money debts, later translated as trespasses or sins. What does forgiveness mean? It is letting someone off the hook even while they still owe you an apology or explanation for their actions.

Forgiving someone does not mean they are welcome back into your life, or that you must fix your relationship with them. It means that you no longer owe each other anything; you are both free. Most of the time, this is why we don’t want to forgive someone: we want them to pay for what they did. When you release the charge you have over them, it completely severs the connection between you, regardless of what they meant to you before.

You are connected to someone as long as you feel like they owe you something. Forgiveness means letting go and ending that connection, even though you might never get that apology, acknowledgment, or explanation. You have lost out on those things, but you have provided yourself with closure and the freedom to move on.

True Forgiveness, Freedom, and Healing

You can choose to forgive someone over and over again, but it is only when you have properly processed your experience that you can truly forgive someone. When you have felt the anger, found the depths of your grief, and found the safety that your nervous system has been craving, you can finally and fully forgive and move on. The beauty and frustration of this experience is that it happens when it happens.

At some point, you realize that something has shifted, and you don’t feel that weight on your chest anymore, or your mind is quieter. It is like noticing that the sun has been shining for a while and smelling the gentle fragrance of new blossoms through the open window. Healing comes as unexpectedly as springtime.

If you work on processing the trauma you went through, at some point, you will no longer flinch when you hear their name, and you will look forward to a new chapter in your future. You cannot decide when you will heal. You can only begin paying attention to your needs and trying to look after yourself. What does forgiveness mean? It means doing the best for yourself and waiting for healing.

We can do a lot of work on our own, but it’s always better when we have others helping us. We host an online catalog of counselors where you can find someone to begin meeting with if you want some extra support. Our reception team would also be happy to help you find the right person for you. Healing and forgiveness are hard and complicated, but you don’t have to be alone on the journey.

item.title: Anger at the Wheel: Signs of an Anger Issue
item.description:
Sometimes, the small things can be indicators of bigger things to come, and what seems innocuous can turn out to be problematic later. Signs of an anger issue might be small or subtle, but they shouldn’t be ignored. When the space shuttle Challenger had an issue with small rubber O-rings (simple circular seals around the diameter of a coin), it led to disaster for the entire crew. Similarly, anger can overthrow a person’s life, causing a lot of damage.

Is anger good or bad?

The word anger might bring up specific images for you. This could be culled from media or perhaps from real-life experiences that you’ve had. Anger is a lot of things, but quite often anger looks and feels ugly. It’s the sort of emotion that might pull us in, but it leaves regret in its wake. Most of us have experienced anger in ourselves or from others, and it’s the sort of experience we’d rather avoid. Anger leaves a bad taste in one’s mouth.

It’s important to remember that anger is a God-given emotion. Like all things the Lord has given us, anger can be turned to ungodly purposes. This doesn’t alter the fact that anger is part of our makeup, and that’s how we were designed. In its proper place, anger alerts us to things being out of alignment, whether that’s injustice, personal boundaries being violated, or because loved ones are in danger of harm and need protection.

Scripture acknowledges anger, and we find Jesus feeling angry at willful blindness as in Mark 3:1-6, for example. There is such a thing as righteous anger, which is anger aroused by an appropriate object or situation and expressed appropriately in turn. God is angry about sin because of how it damages us and the world around us. His anger moves Him to act lovingly, justly, and graciously about that sin.

There is a difference between anger as an emotion, along with the right uses of that anger, and what happens when anger masters you. When anger crosses the line and stops being something that you feel, instead becoming something that rules over or controls you, anger is no longer serving the purpose the Lord set for it. That is when anger erodes relationships, peace, health, and even spiritual witness.

So, is anger good or bad? It’s a bit simplistic putting things that way, but we can talk about it by saying: it depends. Anger can be a good thing when that anger is doing what it is supposed to, but it can also be bad when it gets out of hand and isn’t expressed appropriately.

When anger is in control, it’s dangerous for everyone around you, including yourself. The problem with anger and anger issues is that they are sometimes subtle and don’t announce themselves as we would imagine. That’s why it’s important to know the signs of an anger issue.

The Signs of an Anger Issue

Anger can be subtle, and there are some behaviors that you might not even think of as angry simply because they don’t look like you think anger is supposed to look. Anger issues can creep in bit by bit. They can become normalized by habit, or over time, you can find yourself minimizing them because of feeling shame at what your anger does to you and the people around you. Some signs to look out for include:

Struggling to let things go: It’s not unheard of for someone to carry a grievance for days, weeks, months, or even years. People do cause us harm, but if you find yourself nursing a grudge, replaying offenses in your mind, or building up a mental case against the people who have wronged you, your anger has morphed from being a moment into a stronghold in your life.

Your anger is disproportionate: Being angry is one thing, but it’s important to ask if the anger matches what aroused it, and if the reaction is justified. An anger problem will often reveal itself when there is a consistent mismatch between the trigger for anger and the reaction. When small frustrations regularly produce a firestorm or resentment that lingers, it’s a sign that anger has a hold on you.

Your anger frightens others: It’s worthwhile looking within for the signs of anger issues, but other signs could come from the people around us. How others are around you tells you something important. If your children walk on eggshells around you, if your spouse is anxious in your presence, or if colleagues aren’t eager to collaborate or bring you difficult news because of how you’d react, pay attention to that.

You use anger as a tool: One of the ways anger can be abused is when it starts to function as a means of control and not just as an honest expression of feeling. Anger becomes harmful when it becomes a way of getting what you want from other people. This could look like withdrawing in a cold silence to punish someone, being intimidating to shut down conflict, or raising your voice to make others back down.

Deep regret after anger passes: The Lord made us with the capacity for remorse and to understand the impact our words and actions have on others. If you find yourself regularly making apologies and amends for things you said or did in anger, if you find yourself feeling shame for your actions, but the cycle keeps repeating like a bad dream, that pattern could be pointing to anger issues.

Do you repeatedly regret the way anger leads you to hurt others, but change isn’t forthcoming? The lack of lasting change suggests that the roots of the anger haven’t been unearthed and dealt with.

Anger is affecting your health: Anger isn’t just a mental thing, a set of thoughts roiling around inside of you. Anger is also a physical thing, and it manifests physically through things like a rapid heart rate and clenched muscles. Chronic and unmanaged anger results in tension headaches, trouble sleeping, and high blood pressure. Your body keeps score, telling you that you may have anger issues.

Unhealthy coping mechanisms: The healthy way to deal with anger is to express it in a calm, clear manner that doesn’t blame, shame, or harm others. Suppressing anger, letting anger explode, being passive-aggressive, or directing the anger at yourself are all unhealthy ways of expressing anger. Some people turn to alcohol, food, overwork, or other numbing behaviors to deal with anger, and this isn’t healthy.

Turning to these and other behaviors after an angry episode or when you anticipate such a situation indicates that you’re feeling angry but not processing it properly. Not facing your anger and processing it is a sign that you may have anger issues.

What to Do with Signs of Anger Issues

If you encounter these signs of anger issues in your life, what comes next? For one thing, recognizing these signs shouldn’t be cause for shame. When we fall short, one common response is to withdraw into ourselves or try to hide those shortcomings, perhaps even from ourselves. We might even deflect and try to blame others for it. It’s certainly what the first humans did (Genesis 3:7-13).

Instead of withdrawing, deflecting, or denying, seeing these signs should be seen as an invitation to healing. The Lord wants us to be whole. He wants our lives to be lives of abundant joy, peace, love, patience, self-control, and a lot of other amazing things that are good for us and for the world (Galatians 5:22-26). You don’t have to navigate this journey alone. Christian counseling for anger can be your courageous first step.

Christian counseling for anger can offer you an opportunity and space to work through the roots of your anger. Anger is often not the core issue that’s affecting you; it may be a symptom of deeper wounds such as grief, past trauma, unmet needs, or fear. Counseling is a space where compassion, honesty, and grace are at the foundation, and those wounds can be tended to.

Help is available. You can reach out to our office or browse our online counselor directory to take anger out of the driver’s seat and start moving toward healing and wholeness.

item.title: Anxiety Reduction for First Responders: Finding Peace in High-Pressure Roles
item.description:
The stressors that first responders face are unique to their careers. Their work demands that they be consistently vigilant, quick to make decisions, and emotionally resilient as they face situations where lives are at stake.

Along with this dedication come the challenges that accumulate emotionally and mentally. We don’t always see the internal struggles first responders face daily. Anxiety reduction is vital to helping these individuals maintain focus and clarity as they serve effectively.

The process of managing anxiety includes the acknowledgment that these pressures are real and that seeking support is not a sign of weakness. Intentional strategies that will address anxiety are required for first responders to avoid burnout, compassion fatigue, and diminished capacity to respond effectively in the critical moments of their daily work.

Scripture reminds us that we can come to God with everything we think and feel. “Be anxious for nothing, but in everything by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known to God.” (Philippians 4:6, NASB) This is true for first responders, too.

The Hidden Weight of Constant Readiness

First responders are required to maintain a high-alert mindset. They need to be ready to respond at any moment. This often means that their nervous systems rarely experience true rest. Their daily life has a perpetual readiness woven into every minute, making it difficult to distinguish between on-duty and off-duty.

When the brain adapts to this pattern, there are consequences. Sleep disturbance, irritability, and difficulty relaxing are common experiences that first responders must navigate. Christian counselors understand this hypervigilance and can help navigate intentional counterbalancing practices that allow the body and mind to rest.

There is an unspoken message that surrounds first responders as they absorb the cultural message regarding their profession. That message is that first responders are unshakeable and that displaying any emotional response somehow makes them less able to do their job. This expectation conflicts with human neurobiology. When individuals are repeatedly exposed to traumatic situations, it affects them and everyone around them.

This cultural expectation results in first responders feeling as though they must maintain an image of invulnerability as they struggle with anxiety, intrusive thought patterns, and emotional exhaustion. The disconnect between what they experience internally and what they feel they are permitted to express externally creates additional strain, complicating and compounding the existing stress.

First responders can lean on the promise that “The Lord is near to the brokenhearted and saves those who are crushed in spirit.” (Psalm 34:18, NASB) They don’t need to hide their struggles from Him.

Anxiety Reduction Through Practical Mental Health Strategies

There are specific anxiety-reduction techniques that can benefit first responders when integrated into their daily routine. One effective technique is box breathing, also known as tactical breathing. This breathing technique involves counting to four as the individual inhales, holding for a count of four, exhaling for a count of four, and holding again for a count of four. This can be a real-time tool because it is simple and accessible.

Another technique that can be helpful in anxiety reduction for first responders is progressive muscle relaxation. This helps first responders identify where they are holding tension in their bodies and consciously release it.

Establishing boundaries between work and personal life is a foundation for long-term anxiety management. This requires the individual to create a ritual that signals transitions, such as changing clothes immediately after shifts or engaging in brief physical activity.

These practices can help the nervous system reset and understand that danger has passed and safety has returned. Christian counselors help first responders understand that these boundaries honor their calling to serve and the need to preserve their own well-being.

Sabbath rest speaks directly to the need for rhythms that include cessation from work. When first responders choose to step away from their responsibilities for intentional rest, they are modeling the biblical principle that rest is required to sustain effectiveness. Jesus calls us to Him for rest when we are weary. “Come to Me, all who are weary and heavy-laden, and I will give you rest.” (Matthew 11:28, NASB)

The Role of Connection and Community

First responders often feel isolated because they cannot share their experiences with people outside their field. Having a peer support group that allows them to share with others who understand gives them a space for honest conversation. These connections remind them that their responses are normal reactions to abnormal circumstances. When they gather with others who understand the unique pressures of their work, the weight of carrying these experiences alone begins to diminish.

Engaging in professional mental health support tailored for first responders can offer a crucial layer of care. Therapists and counselors who specialize in trauma and occupational stress understand the specific challenges involved with being a first responder. Through evidence-based treatments integrated with faith-based support, a way to address trauma symptoms directly is created.

Engaging with this professional support demonstrates wisdom rather than weakness. It shows a commitment to maintaining the capacity to serve in the long term. The decision to seek professional help allows first responders to process what they have experienced during their shifts in a safe environment where their vulnerability is respected, and healing is prioritized.

Working with a Christian counselor embodies the directive in Ecclesiastes. “Two are better than one because they have a good return for their labor. For if either of them falls, the one will lift up his companion.” (Ecclesiastes 4:9-10, NASB) A counselor can be there to support first responders in their struggles.

Physical Health as a Foundation for Anxiety Reduction

The connection between physical health and mental well-being is particularly important for first responders. Regular exercise can provide a healthy outlet for processing stress and hormones and improve overall resilience to anxiety. Cardiovascular exercise, strength training, and flexibility all contribute to better stress regulation. First responders often find that establishing a consistent exercise routine creates structure and predictability for those with unpredictable schedules.

First responders have irregular schedules that often disrupt their sleep patterns, which impacts anxiety levels. When first responders are able to maintain consistent sleep at night by creating dark, cool sleep environments, they can improve their sleep quality even with their challenging schedules.

Eating balanced meals to stabilize blood sugar prevents symptoms of anxiety from compounding the mental and emotional load. These practical steps create a foundation that supports anxiety reduction and helps first responders maintain the physical stamina their work demands. They can care for their body as the temple God says it is to help them withstand the challenges of their work.

Or do you not know that your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit who is in you, whom you have from God, and that you are not your own? – 1 Corinthians 6:19, NASB

Sustainable Service Through Self-Care

First responders are professionals whose work holds immense value. They choose to protect and serve communities in the most vulnerable moments. But sustaining the service throughout their careers requires acknowledging that even the strongest individual needs support.

Anxiety reduction involves developing practices and support systems that prevent anxiety from becoming overwhelming and debilitating. Christian counselors work with first responders to create personalized approaches that will honor their professional calling and the human need for care.

Navigating toward better mental health in the demanding roles of first responders starts with recognizing that seeking help reflects strength and wisdom. This requires implementing practical strategies and addressing deeper patterns of thought and belief that influence how first responders relate to their experiences.

Faith offers a framework for understanding that human limitations are part of the design, and a reminder that dependence on God isn’t weakness but the pathway to enduring strength. When first responders prioritize their mental health through anxiety-reduction practices, they are positioning themselves to serve more effectively and sustainably.
